title: Automate Gemini 4 Neon: How to Set It Up (2026 Guide)
summary: Automate Gemini 4 Neon workflows to send data to Gemini and store results in Neon Postgres. Use Activepieces or code to build this integration.
body_markdown:
## Build the Gemini to Neon workflow in Activepieces


Build it in four stages, and don't move to the next until the current one has run once with real data and left a visible result: a stored sample, a text reply, a database row, a failure notice.


[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/) has Google Gemini and PostgreSQL integrations, and Neon is Postgres, so the trigger, Gemini call and row write above is a task it covers directly.


You can also skip the stages by describing that pipeline in its built-in chat, which publishes a live flow in your account, the same artifact you would have assembled by hand.


Because the flow is an ordinary one, it gets the same RBAC, audit logs and run traces as anything built manually, so the run trace shows what each step did and a row that never landed can be traced to the step that failed.


MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run Activepieces in production.


### Stage 1: trigger that fires and stores sample data


Start with a Web Form trigger, because you can fire it yourself from a browser and need no outside system.


In the CV Scanning flow below, the first step is a Web Form labeled "Human Input".


Its panel lists a published and a draft form URL, and a warning about "Wait for Response", so you know which URL is for testing and that a form left waiting will hold the caller open.


Use the draft URL, submit one realistic entry, then press Test Trigger.


Swap the sheet and PDF steps in that example for Gemini and Neon, and the trigger works the same way. Stop when the sample data shows your submitted fields, because every later step maps from that sample.


### Stage 2: Gemini step that returns text


Add the Google Gemini step, connect your API key, and choose a model. Gemini 3 Flash is a sensible default for a text task like this, since it's low-cost and fast.


Put the form field into the prompt by selecting it from the trigger's sample data, not by typing the placeholder by hand. Run the step on its own.


Stop when you can read Gemini's reply in the step output.


If it errors here, the cause is almost always the key or a quota on your Google project, not the flow. Fix it now, because a quota error will look identical later and be harder to trace.


### Stage 3: write the result as a Neon row


Because Neon is Postgres, you connect through a Postgres step using the connection string from your Neon project. Create the target table first, with a text column for the input, a text column for Gemini's reply, and a timestamp.


Map the trigger field and the Gemini output into those columns, then test the step.


Stop when the row appears in Neon's table viewer. Expect a slow or failed first attempt if the database has been idle, since a suspended Neon compute has to wake before it accepts the connection. That is the failure the next stage exists for.


### Add retries and failure alerts to the workflow


Turn on retry for the Gemini and database steps, so a cold database or a brief rate limit gets a second attempt rather than ending the run.


Then set the steps to continue on failure and route the failed path to a Slack or email step that names the flow and the step.


You find it a week later, in an empty table: the flow that failed silently.
